events.title: The Pequot War and the Mystic massacre
events.place: Mystic River, Connecticut, and southern New England
events.summary: In 1636–1638 the English colonies of New England and their Narragansett and Mohegan allies destroyed the Pequot nation; at Mystic on May 26, 1637 colonists set the Pequot fort ablaze and killed between 400 and 700 people, and hundreds of captives were enslaved.

On the night of May 26, 1637 a Connecticut force under Captain John Mason, joined by Captain John Underhill and allied Natives, surrounded the fortified Pequot village near the Mystic River; Mason ordered it set ablaze and its two exits blocked, and those who tried to escape over the palisade were shot or killed outside. Between 400 and 700 Pequots were killed. Underhill wrote that “there were about foure hundred soules in this Fort, and not above five of them escaped out of our hands.”

By the end of the war about 700 Pequots had been killed or taken captive. Hundreds of prisoners were enslaved; most were sold to colonists in Bermuda or the West Indies, and others were given as captives to the Narragansett and Mohegan. The Treaty of Hartford of 1638 forbade the Pequots to return to their lands, speak their language or call themselves Pequots, and the colonial authorities classed them as extinct; a western band kept its sovereignty and is today a federally recognized nation.

events.title: The Supreme Court’s Indian cases: discovery, dependency and Worcester
events.place: Washington, D.C.; the Cherokee Nation, Georgia
events.summary: In three cases Chief Justice John Marshall’s court laid down the doctrine of discovery (1823), called the Cherokee a “domestic dependent nation” (1831), and upheld Cherokee sovereignty against Georgia (1832), a ruling that did not save them from removal.
account: In Johnson v. M’Intosh (1823) Marshall set out the “discovery doctrine”: a European power gains sovereignty over the land it discovers and the exclusive right to extinguish the Native occupants’ “right of occupancy”. In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (March 18, 1831) he held that the Cherokee Nation was not a foreign nation but a “domestic dependent nation”, its relation to the United States like that of “a ward to its guardian”.

In Worcester v. Georgia (March 3, 1832) the Court struck down Georgia’s law barring non-Natives from Cherokee land without a state license, building the foundations of tribal sovereignty. Jackson wrote that the decision “has fell still born”; the words “John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it!” are believed to be apocryphal. On December 29, 1835 a few Cherokees without authority signed the removal Treaty of New Echota; Justice Stephen Breyer later observed that the Cherokee nation was the “obvious loser”.

events.title: McGirt v. Oklahoma
events.summary: On July 9, 2020 the Supreme Court held that the reservation promised to the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in the 19th century was never disestablished and remains Indian country, so Oklahoma could not prosecute Native people for major crimes there.
account: Before statehood in 1907 about half of Oklahoma, including Tulsa, belonged to the Five Tribes: the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Muscogee Creek and Seminole. The case was brought by Jimcy McGirt, an enrolled member of the Seminole tribe. Writing for a 5–4 majority, Justice Gorsuch held that the Muscogee domain remains Indian country under the Major Crimes Act: “Because Congress has not said otherwise, we hold the government to its word.” He rejected the argument that “the price of keeping” the promises “has become too great.”

Oklahoma’s Court of Criminal Appeals applied McGirt to rule that nine other nations’ reservations had not been disestablished, but held it was not retroactive. In Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta (2022) the Supreme Court held that the state shares jurisdiction over crimes by non-Natives against Natives in Indian country.
